In RE, the channels are cleanly separable---confusability drives substitution errors while detection remains stable. In NER, Channel~2 additionally impairs entity detection, suggesting that for span-level extraction, type ambiguity and boundary ambiguity are coupled.

105	Per-type analysis on MAVEN reveals an anomaly: the correlation between mean BCS and per-type error rate is \emph{positive}---Qwen3 $\rho = +0.184$ ($p = 0.025$) and MiniLM $\rho = +0.208$ ($p = 0.011$)---opposite to the negative direction predicted by the confusability hypothesis.
106	
107	This reversal traces to a property of same-domain schemas documented by \citet{cai-isotropy-clusters-2021}: when all types derive from a single ontology (here, FrameNet), their embeddings collapse into a single cluster in representation space. In this regime, a type's mean BCS conflates two distinct properties: (i)~confusability with neighbors, which should increase errors, and (ii)~centrality within the cluster, which correlates with being a well-represented, high-frequency type that LLMs extract reliably. The centrality signal dominates, flipping the aggregate correlation.
108

110	
111	Few-NERD, whose 66 types span 8 coarse categories across diverse domains, does not exhibit this confound. Its per-type correlation is $\rho = -0.293$ ($p = 0.02$, $n = 63$), in the expected negative direction: types with higher mean confusability have higher error rates. The cross-domain schema spans multiple embedding clusters, breaking the centrality--confusability conflation.
112	
113	This analysis carries a practical implication: mean BCS is a reliable predictor of schema difficulty only for cross-domain schemas. For same-domain schemas where types form a single semantic cluster, pairwise SCS should be used directly, or the centrality component must be factored out before aggregation. A residualized partial-correlation analysis confirming that the raw BCS--F1 correlation vanishes after controlling for frequency and degree centrality is provided in Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_residualized_bcs}.

These results establish two degradation channels: \textbf{Channel~1} (count $\to$ recall decline, \S\ref{sec:count_curves}) and \textbf{Channel~2} (confusability $\to$ type confusion). In RE, the channels are cleanly separable---confusability drives substitution errors while detection remains stable. In NER, Channel~2 additionally impairs entity detection, suggesting that for span-level extraction, type ambiguity and boundary ambiguity are coupled.

\subsection{Centrality Confound on Homogeneous Schemas}
\label{sec:centrality_confound}

Per-type analysis on MAVEN reveals an anomaly: the correlation between mean BCS and per-type error rate is \emph{positive}---Qwen3 $\rho = +0.184$ ($p = 0.025$) and MiniLM $\rho = +0.208$ ($p = 0.011$)---opposite to the negative direction predicted by the confusability hypothesis.

This reversal traces to a property of same-domain schemas documented by \citet{cai-isotropy-clusters-2021}: when all types derive from a single ontology (here, FrameNet), their embeddings collapse into a single cluster in representation space. In this regime, a type's mean BCS conflates two distinct properties: (i)~confusability with neighbors, which should increase errors, and (ii)~centrality within the cluster, which correlates with being a well-represented, high-frequency type that LLMs extract reliably. The centrality signal dominates, flipping the aggregate correlation.

Critically, the pairwise SCS--confusion correlation remains intact: MAVEN MiniLM pairwise $r = 0.129$ (CI: [0.104, 0.156], $p < 10^{-10}$), consistent with the values in Table~\ref{tab:pairwise}. The problem lies in the aggregation step (mean BCS per type), not in the pairwise signal itself.

Few-NERD, whose 66 types span 8 coarse categories across diverse domains, does not exhibit this confound. Its per-type correlation is $\rho = -0.293$ ($p = 0.02$, $n = 63$), in the expected negative direction: types with higher mean confusability have higher error rates. The cross-domain schema spans multiple embedding clusters, breaking the centrality--confusability conflation.

This analysis carries a practical implication: mean BCS is a reliable predictor of schema difficulty only for cross-domain schemas. For same-domain schemas where types form a single semantic cluster, pairwise SCS should be used directly, or the centrality component must be factored out before aggregation. A residualized partial-correlation analysis confirming that the raw BCS--F1 correlation vanishes after controlling for frequency and degree centrality is provided in Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_residualized_bcs}.

Taken together, these results establish two orthogonal degradation channels: \textbf{Channel~1} (count $\to$ recall decline, \S\ref{sec:count_curves}) and \textbf{Channel~2} (confusability $\to$ type confusion, this section). The channels are mechanistically distinct---Channel~1 reflects capacity limits as more types compete for attention, while Channel~2 reflects semantic similarity making types indistinguishable regardless of count.

\subsection{Centrality Confound on Homogeneous Schemas}
\label{sec:centrality_confound}

Per-type analysis on MAVEN reveals an anomaly: the correlation between mean BCS and per-type error rate is \emph{positive}---Qwen3 $\rho = +0.189$ ($p = 0.021$) and MiniLM $\rho = +0.208$ ($p = 0.011$)---opposite to the negative direction predicted by the confusability hypothesis.

This reversal traces to a property of same-domain schemas documented by \citet{cai-isotropy-clusters-2021}: when all types derive from a single ontology (here, FrameNet), their embeddings collapse into a single cluster in representation space. In this regime, a type's mean BCS conflates two distinct properties: (i)~confusability with neighbors, which should increase errors, and (ii)~centrality within the cluster, which correlates with being a well-represented, high-frequency type that LLMs extract reliably. The centrality signal dominates, flipping the aggregate correlation.

Critically, the pairwise SCS--confusion correlation remains intact: MAVEN MiniLM pairwise $r = 0.129$ (CI: [0.104, 0.156], $p < 10^{-10}$), consistent with the values in Table~\ref{tab:pairwise}. The problem lies in the aggregation step (mean BCS per type), not in the pairwise signal itself.

Few-NERD, whose 66 types span 8 coarse categories across diverse domains, does not exhibit this confound. Its per-type correlation is $\rho = -0.293$ ($p = 0.02$, $n = 63$), in the expected negative direction: types with higher mean confusability have higher error rates. The cross-domain schema spans multiple embedding clusters, breaking the centrality--confusability conflation.

This analysis carries a practical implication: mean BCS is a reliable predictor of schema difficulty only for cross-domain schemas. For same-domain schemas where types form a single semantic cluster, pairwise SCS should be used directly, or the centrality component must be factored out before aggregation.

104	\label{sec:centrality_confound}
105	
106	Per-type analysis on MAVEN reveals an anomaly: the correlation between mean BCS and per-type error rate is \emph{positive}---Qwen3 $\rho = +0.184$ ($p = 0.025$) and MiniLM $\rho = +0.208$ ($p = 0.011$)---opposite to the negative direction predicted by the confusability hypothesis.
107	
108	This reversal traces to a property of same-domain schemas documented by \citet{cai-isotropy-clusters-2021}: when all types derive from a single ontology (here, FrameNet), their embeddings collapse into a single cluster in representation space. In this regime, a type's mean BCS conflates two distinct properties: (i)~confusability with neighbors, which should increase errors, and (ii)~centrality within the cluster, which correlates with being a well-represented, high-frequency type that LLMs extract reliably. The centrality signal dominates, flipping the aggregate correlation.
